passage: I'm Pema, and in my second week at the start-up I noticed what nobody said out loud. The office lights were still on at ten every night, and people ate dinner at their desks. When the founder walked past, keyboards got louder. A missed target meant a group email naming the person. I asked Ganga, who sat beside me, whether it was always like this. She shrugged: “It's just how it is. You get used to it.” Around us, everybody nodded slightly, as if we were talking about the weather. I felt a strange dizziness, as if I'd walked into a room where everyone else could breathe underwater. I'm writing this down now because I suspect that in a month I won't see it at all.

qa.q: What happened when the founder walked past?
qa.a: The keyboards got louder when the founder walked past.

qa.q: What does Pema's “strange dizziness” suggest about how Pema feels in the office?
qa.a: Pema feels startled and out of step, because the long hours and fear of blame seem ordinary to everyone else but not to a newcomer.

qa.q: What could Pema do to keep the clear view Pema has now?
qa.a: Pema could keep writing down what stands out, talk to someone outside the company and check what feels normal with people from other workplaces.

qa.q: What might Ganga be feeling when she says, “You get used to it”?
qa.a: Ganga may have accepted the routine as the price of staying and may be trying to comfort Pema, without noticing how much she has adjusted.

grounding: A newcomer sees long hours, fear of the leadership and blame as ordinary because everyone else accepts them, and knows blending in would remove the clarity.

passage:
Onboarding coach's note, week 5.
Pema, who joined as an analyst, said in her first week, “Is it normal that nobody leaves before the director does?” I have watched her since. In week two she was still asking questions in team meetings. By week three she was eating lunch at her desk like the rest. Yesterday, when the director named a colleague in a group email for a missed number, everyone looked at their screens, and Pema did too. Afterwards she said, “I guess this is just how it works here.” I asked what she had noticed in week one. She paused a long time. I've suggested she write down what she sees, and we will talk next Friday.
Tushar

qa.q: What did Pema ask in the first week?
qa.a: Pema asked, “Is it normal that nobody leaves before the director does?”

qa.q: What might Pema be feeling when Pema says, “I guess this is just how it works here”?
qa.a: Pema may be giving in to the group's view and feeling some doubt, since the fresh clarity of week one has faded.

qa.q: What did Tushar suggest to help Pema keep seeing clearly?
qa.a: Tushar suggested that Pema write down what she sees and planned to talk again next Friday.

qa.q: What might it be like for the colleague named in the group email when everyone looked at their screens?
qa.a: That colleague may feel exposed and alone, since nobody spoke up or even looked up, and the silence makes the blame seem normal.

grounding: A newcomer sees fear of the leadership and blame as ordinary because everyone accepts them, and blending in slowly removes the clarity, seen by an onboarding coach.
